WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000734.subject: longevity
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000734.question: Does meditation reduce the risk of cancer and heart disease?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000734.answer_short: Wallach cites studies that meditation cuts cancer risk 55% and heart disease 80%, while raising DHEA and lowering cortisol.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000734.answer_full:
Yes — Wallach cites several studies reporting that meditation cuts the risk of cancer by 55% and heart disease by 80%, and he treats it as a genuine anti-aging practice rather than just a way to relax. His reasoning runs through your hormones: meditation raises circulating DHEA, which he calls the "youth hormone," while lowering cortisol, which he describes as "age-inducing." Alongside that it lowers blood pressure and relaxes the muscles — a combination he says supports the body's rejuvenating processes.

That logic fits his wider view that aging itself is a driver of these very diseases. Elsewhere Wallach reads the visible marks of aging — the "age spots" or "liver spots" on older skin — as the outward tip of internal decay that, in his account, sharply raises the risk of cancer, Alzheimer's, and heart disease. Seen through that lens, anything that slows the aging process — including tamping down "age-inducing" cortisol — is working against the same cancer and heart-disease risk.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000738.subject: minerals
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000738.question: Why did the Navajo become obese and diabetic?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000738.answer_short: In the 1940s urban Navajo cooks swapped mineral-rich cooking wood ash for baking soda, and Wallach ties the rise of obesity and diabetes to that loss of dietary minerals.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000738.answer_full:
Wallach traces it to a single 1940s substitution. As urban Navajo cooks switched to electricity and gas, they stopped adding the mineral-rich "culinary" wood ash their tradition called for and reached instead for the more available — but mineral-poor — baking soda. That swap, he says, marks the turn from the slim, wood-ash-using Navajo shepherds to the obese and diabetic, baking-soda-using urban Navajo.

The reason it matters is that Wallach frames obesity as a mineral-deficiency disease, "not a disease of excess." In his telling, when a diet loses its trace minerals the body keeps hunting for them: empty-calorie food triggers "pica," a compulsive nibbling driven by the search for those missing minerals, so people overeat and gain weight. He calls the broader pattern the "Feedlot Syndrome" — people put on a mineral-depleted diet, stripped of their traditional "culinary" and garden ashes, gain weight unless they consciously supplement with plant minerals.

The mirror image, in his account, is the Old Order Amish: they eat more sugar, fat, red meat and dairy than almost anyone, yet their obesity rate runs about 4% and their type-II diabetes rate about 6% — roughly a tenth and a half, respectively, of their modern neighbors in the very same county. He credits that gap not to their diet, nor even to their farm labor, but to the essential minerals in the wood ashes they spread on their garden soil every morning — the same minerals the urban Navajo gave up.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000747.subject: hunza
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000747.question: Do the Hunza have birth defects?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000747.answer_short: Almost never - Wallach says only two 'mukhanas' (hermaphrodites) were recorded in Hunza's entire 2,300-year history.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000747.answer_full:
Almost never. Wallach reports that congenital abnormality is virtually unknown among the Hunza — in the entire 2,300-year history of this famously long-lived people, only two "mukhanas," or hermaphrodites, have ever been recorded.

For Wallach that near-total absence isn't luck — it's the flip side of his whole theory of birth defects. He argues that congenital defects, intersex anatomy included, aren't inborn genetic bad luck but the result of nutritional deficiency in the mother during early embryonic development. He leans on veterinary evidence to make the point: animals routinely show unusual sexual anatomy and congenital defects when the embryo is starved of nutrients, and in his telling every known congenital defect of the human sexual organs has also been recorded in animals. By that logic a population that is exceptionally well-nourished should almost never produce such defects — and the Hunza, he says, are exactly that. Anyone who survives the first year of life typically lives past eighty in excellent health, with many reaching their nineties and past 100, and disease is so rare that the main cause of premature death is accidents like landslides and falls rather than illness. Wallach's one-word explanation for that whole picture is minerals — the thing he calls the real Fountain of Youth.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000752.subject: diabetes
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000752.question: Does bitter melon help with blood sugar or diabetes?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000752.answer_short: Wallach says bitter melon (Goya), an Okinawan staple, is known to support healthy blood sugar levels in diabetics.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000752.answer_full:
Yes. Wallach says bitter melon — known as Goya in Okinawa, botanically Momordica charantia, a lumpy vegetable he describes as looking like a cucumber with warts — is known to support healthy blood sugar levels in diabetics. He frames that as an "added benefit" of a food eaten mainly as a staple: it's a mainstay of the Okinawan diet, which he ate a lot of himself while visiting, thought to have been brought to the Ryukyu Kingdom from old China during the Ming and Manchu dynasties and used as a food staple since around 1100 A.D.

That Okinawan connection matters to him, because Wallach points to the Okinawans as the longest-lived people in the industrialized world — ranked so by the World Health Organization in 1996 — and bitter melon sits right on their table. Still, in his telling it's a supportive food rather than the centerpiece: his actual blood-sugar "magic bullets" for diabetes are the minerals chromium and vanadium, the latter of which he says works like insulin.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000757.subject: resveratrol
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000757.question: What is the Grape Cure?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000757.answer_short: A 1928 book by Johanna Brandt claiming dark red grapes benefit cancer, heart disease and diabetes; Wallach cites it as an early sign of what we now call resveratrol.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000757.answer_full:
The Grape Cure is a 1928 book by Johanna Brandt, a South African healer, who claimed that dark red grapes could benefit a whole collection of diseases — cancer, heart disease and diabetes among them. Wallach cites it as the historical seed of red wine's longevity benefit. Brandt was branded a charlatan by the local medical associations and chased out of the United States, but Wallach's point is that she was onto something real: "there was something in those red grapes."

In his modern telling, that hunch holds up. Wallach considers moderate red wine preferable to complete abstinence — he credits it with reducing vascular inflammation and lowering the risk of coronary heart disease and cancer, and with significantly increasing longevity across a striking range of creatures, from yeast, worms and flies to fish and small mammals including primates.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000764.subject: resveratrol
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000764.question: Does resveratrol affect amyloid-beta or Alzheimer's plaques?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000764.answer_short: A 2005 study Wallach cites found resveratrol significantly lowers secreted and intracellular amyloid-beta (Abeta) peptides, the peptides tied to Alzheimer's.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000764.answer_full:
Yes — Wallach cites a study, published in the November 11, 2005 issue of the Journal of Biological Chemistry, in which researchers found that resveratrol significantly lowered the levels of amyloid-beta (Abeta) peptides. The drop covered both the "secreted" form (Abeta released outside the cell) and the "intracellular" form (the portion held inside it), and it showed up across several different cell lines rather than in just one — so the effect wasn't a quirk of a single cell type.

He folds this into a wider case that Alzheimer's is a preventable, nutrition-driven condition rather than a sentence. In the same vein he points to a 2004 Johns Hopkins study of nearly 5,000 people over 65 in which a special diet plus nutrient supplementation cut Alzheimer's risk by 78%, and to a finding that diets rich in omega-3 fatty acids reduced the risk of dementia by 48%. He also pushes back on the popular fear that aluminum causes Alzheimer's, citing a 1992 Oxford study that found identical brain-aluminum levels in patients and controls — for Wallach the lever is what nutrition can add, not a metal to avoid.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000767.subject: resveratrol
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000767.question: Can resveratrol offset the harm of a high-fat diet?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000767.answer_short: In a Harvard/NIA mouse study, resveratrol let high-fat-fed mice avoid insulin resistance, heart disease and liver damage and cut their death risk by 31%.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000767.answer_full:
Yes — at least in the animal study Wallach points to. In a Harvard Medical School and National Institute of Aging experiment, mice were kept on a high-fat, high-calorie diet, but some of them also received resveratrol. After a year, the resveratrol group had stayed healthy: they never developed the insulin resistance, heart disease or liver damage that struck their high-fat-fed counterparts, and they carried a 31% lower risk of death. What makes it striking is that the diet itself never improved — the resveratrol appeared to blunt the harm of all that fat and calories on its own.

It's a pattern Wallach returns to, where a single compound quietly lowers the same cluster of killer diseases. He cites Norman Hollenberg of Harvard, who found that the island-dwelling Kuna people, who drink flavanol-rich cocoa, carry a 10% lower risk of four of the five biggest killers — stroke, heart failure, cancer and diabetes — a result Hollenberg thought might rank among the most important observations in the history of medicine. He points, too, to a 2006 study crediting coffee's antioxidants with a lower risk of diabetes, heart disease and rheumatoid arthritis.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000771.subject: chocolate
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000771.question: Is dark chocolate good for weight loss and energy?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000771.answer_short: Chocolate's cocoagin, theobromine, flavanol and flavonoids are thermogenic and antioxidant, making bitter chocolate an energy generator, weight-loss aid and free-radical neutralizer.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000771.answer_full:
Yes — in Wallach's framing, dark (bitter) chocolate helps on both fronts at once. He calls it a rich source of cocoagin, caffeine, theobromine, flavanol and flavonoids, and says these compounds carry two kinds of power: thermogenic properties, meaning they generate energy and heat (the engine behind both the energy lift and the fat-burning), and antioxidant properties, meaning they neutralize free radicals. That pairing is why he rates bitter chocolate a great energy generator, a great weight-loss product, and — in his words — a super free-radical-neutralizing herb.

The two effects reinforce each other. Wallach warns that shedding weight by burning body fat itself throws off free-radical damage, so a food that both burns and mops up free radicals in the same bite is doing double duty. The flavonoids doing the mopping are the plant compounds he once knew as 'vitamin P' — antioxidant and anti-inflammatory — and he puts the ideal daily antioxidant intake at 20,000 to 25,000 ORAC points.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000772.subject: antioxidants
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000772.question: What are the health benefits of anthocyanins?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000772.answer_short: Anthocyanins repair free-radical damage to small blood vessels, block histamine, and fight the inflammation behind atherosclerosis, arthritis, gastric ulcers and diabetes.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000772.answer_full:
Their standout benefit, in Wallach's telling, is that anthocyanins don't merely prevent free-radical damage to the small blood vessels — they actually repair it, which he calls unusual. That matters because he pins inflamed, damaged blood-vessel walls as the direct cause of atherosclerosis (fatty plaque building up in the arteries), coronary thrombosis (a clot blocking a heart artery) and stroke — so anthocyanins act at the root of those conditions rather than their symptoms.

Wallach also credits them with blocking the histamine response — the trigger behind allergic reactions — and with calming inflammation and irritation. And he points to studies showing anthocyanins can halt the inflammation tied to arthritis, gastric ulcers, diabetes and cardiovascular disease. That fits his larger stance that heart disease isn't something you simply inherit: he frames cardiovascular disease as a cluster of conditions driven by free-radical damage to the artery lining plus specific nutrient shortfalls — exactly the vessel-wall damage anthocyanins are working to prevent and repair.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000773.subject: chocolate
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000773.question: Do catechins in chocolate help prevent cancer?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000773.answer_short: The catechins and epicatechins in chocolate prevent carcinogen formation and drive the body's own detoxification and defenses.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000773.answer_full:
Yes — Wallach counts catechins and epicatechins, the phytonutrients (beneficial plant compounds) in chocolate, as part of what he calls chocolate's "disease-relieving arsenal." He credits them with anti-cancer work on two fronts. First, they help block the creation of carcinogens — cancer-causing chemicals — in the first place. Second, they switch on and support the body's own built-in "detoxification" and defense processes, so it clears threats more effectively.

To see what "blocking the creation of carcinogens" means in his framework, look at how a carcinogen actually gets made: Wallach explains that the nitrites and nitrates used to preserve cured meats like bacon, ham and deli slices are converted, in the acid of the stomach, into nitrosamines — compounds that can in turn become cancer-causing chemicals. Stopping formation like that, before the carcinogen even exists, is the kind of protection he attributes to chocolate's catechins.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000777.subject: chocolate
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000777.question: What kind of fat is in chocolate?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000777.answer_short: Cacao butter is stearic acid (34%), palmitic acid (20%) and oleic acid (30%) - the oleic acid being the same mono-unsaturated fat found in olive oil.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000777.answer_full:
The fat in chocolate is cacao butter, and Wallach breaks it into three main fatty acids: stearic acid (34%), palmitic acid (20%) and oleic acid (30%). Stearic and palmitic are the saturated fats in the mix, while oleic acid is a mono-unsaturated fat — the same kind that makes up olive oil.

What makes this more than trivia, in his telling, is that chocolate's fat may not be the villain it's assumed to be. Wallach cites a Harvard School of Public Health review of 136 studies which found that stearic acid — chocolate's primary fat — has no adverse effect on blood vessels, cholesterol or overall cardiovascular health, because the body metabolizes it differently than other saturated fats. The same review flagged chocolate as a major source of flavonoids (the plant antioxidants epicatechins, catechins and procyanidins).

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000778.subject: chocolate
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000778.question: Does chocolate raise cholesterol?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000778.answer_short: Studies Wallach cites say chocolate doesn't raise cholesterol or LDL and that cacao flavonoids boost blood flow to the heart, brain, hands and legs.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000778.answer_full:
No — Wallach cites studies published in the Journal of the American College of Nutrition reporting that chocolate does not raise cholesterol or increase LDL cholesterol. His explanation comes down to the kind of fat chocolate carries. Pointing to a Harvard School of Public Health review of 136 studies, he notes that chocolate's primary fat, stearic acid, is metabolized differently from other saturated fats — so it doesn't have the adverse effects on blood vessels, cholesterol, or overall cardiovascular health you'd expect from a saturated fat.

That same review flags chocolate as a major source of flavonoids — plant compounds like epicatechins, catechins and procyanidins — and this is where Wallach sees an actual upside rather than just a neutral verdict. Citing a 2003 report in the journal Hypertension, he says cacao's flavonoids can help increase blood flow to the heart, brain, hands and legs. More broadly, he holds that flavonoids reduce cardiovascular risk: they inhibit clotting, thrombus formation and platelet aggregation, reduce atherosclerosis, and lower blood pressure.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000806.subject: sulfur
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000806.question: What nutrient keeps spinal discs and cartilage from breaking down?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000806.answer_short: Wallach says sulfur — as chondroitin sulfate — is built into the discs, cartilage, tendons and ligaments, and a sulfur deficiency causes osteoarthritis, osteoporosis and cartilage degeneration.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000806.answer_full:
Wallach's answer is sulfur — specifically the sulfur locked into chondroitin sulfate, the compound that forms your cartilage, ligaments, tendons, spinal discs and connective tissue. Because sulfur is built structurally into that tissue, running short of it lets the whole framework break down: he says a sulfur deficiency produces osteoarthritis, osteoporosis, degeneration of the cartilage, and weakened tendons and ligaments. The same shortfall, in his telling, feeds the "collagen diseases" like lupus and sickle-cell anemia.

This is why Wallach singles out sulfur for the degenerative kinds of arthritis — the joint wear where the cartilage itself is wasting away — and names it alongside calcium, magnesium, boron and copper as the cluster of mineral deficiencies behind arthritis. His approach is to rebuild the tissue rather than mask the pain: his arthritis protocol feeds the joints cartilage directly — collagen, glucosamine sulfate and chondroitin sulfate — at 1,000 mg three times a day.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000809.subject: malnutrition
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000809.question: Can crash dieting or not eating enough lower your sex drive?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000809.answer_short: Yes — Wallach says a calorie-cut diet without full nutrition produces malnutrition that reduces libido and causes infertility, so starving yourself backfires on your sex drive.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000809.answer_full:
Yes — but Wallach draws a sharp line: it isn't the calorie cut itself that wrecks your sex drive, it's cutting calories without keeping the nutrition up. His whole longevity approach rests on "under-nutrition without malnutrition" — you can eat less (he puts the target at 1,250 to 1,800 calories a day) as long as you still supply every essential nutrient at optimal levels, with a special focus on minerals. The problem, he says, is that most people forget that second half.

When they do, the body slides into what he calls diseases of malnutrition: reduced libido, menstrual problems (dysmenorrhea, or painful periods), and infertility, along with a real drop in bone density and wide swings in body temperature. So starving yourself doesn't just fail to help — in his telling it actively backfires on your sex life and fertility.

For men, Wallach adds a hormonal reason. The body manufactures testosterone out of cholesterol, so a diet that pushes cholesterol too low drags testosterone down with it — and, in his words, leaves a man "totally disinterested in sex." Under-eating strips out the very raw materials the sex hormones are built from.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000810.subject: gout
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000810.question: Is gout caused by rich living and overeating?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000810.answer_short: Wallach cites Luigi Cornaro, whose gluttonous, intemperate life made him obese and gouty by 37 - framing gout as a disease of over-indulgence.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000810.answer_full:
Yes — Wallach frames gout as a classic disease of intemperate living, and his example is Luigi Cornaro, an Italian nobleman whose "dissolute, gluttonous" habits had wrecked his health by the age of 37. In Wallach's telling the overindulgence didn't just bring on gout; it produced a whole cluster of ailments at once. Cornaro was morbidly obese, suffered gout and recurrent "stomach fever," ran cold all the time (which Wallach reads as hypothyroidism, an underactive thyroid), and lived with generalized pain he attributes to arthritis and fibromyalgia. The point of the anecdote is that gout travels with the lifestyle rather than striking at random.

It fits Wallach's broader conviction that diet, not medicine, decides who gets sick: he cites a 1990 survey by Lucian Lepe finding that America's shortest-lived counties were the fried-food regions of the old South and the western reservations — the nation's heart-attack, stroke, diabetes, obesity and cancer belt — while the longest-lived were Scandinavian-heritage dairy-farming communities who poached, stewed, roasted and baked their food.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000811.subject: longevity
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000811.question: Can changing your diet turn gout around?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000811.answer_short: Wallach's gout example, Luigi Cornaro, reversed a life of ill health with a temperate, calorie-restricted diet - becoming lean and living to 103.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000811.answer_full:
Wallach's answer is yes, and his standing proof is Luigi Cornaro — a man who turned his health around by switching to a temperate, calorie-restricted diet and staying with it for the rest of his life. Despite hard-living younger years, Cornaro became lean and watched his health prosper, living to 103 and never retiring: he worked his estate from horseback, counseled the Paduan society as a revered elder, and wrote books on health right to the end.

The lever in his story is what Wallach calls calorie restriction WITHOUT malnutrition — the distinction he says most people who attempt it miss entirely. He puts the level at 1,250 to 1,800 calories a day (those doing heavier physical labor at the upper end), the common thread he finds among centenarians historically and in every modern Blue Zone. The "without malnutrition" half is the catch: every essential nutrient at optimal levels, well above the RDI, packed into fewer calories. And he attaches a concrete payoff — a 150-to-175-pound person can add 25 to 50 HEALTHFUL years, not years of decline, by pairing that diet with a faithful supplement program, with the lower food bill more than covering the cost of the supplements.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000812.subject: antioxidants
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000812.question: Do anthocyanins or colorful fruits help with allergies?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000812.answer_short: The anthocyanin pigments in deep-colored berries and fruit can block histamine and calm allergic reactions, according to Wallach.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000812.answer_full:
Yes — Wallach says the anthocyanins, the pigments that give deeply colored fruits like berries their rich hue, can block the histamine response and in doing so calm allergic reactions, inflammation and irritation. Histamine is the compound the body releases during an allergic reaction — the trigger behind the itchy, runny, inflamed flare — and in Wallach's framework the body builds it from the amino acid histidine. Blocking that histamine response turns the reaction down closer to its source.

He also frames anthocyanins as protectors of the small blood vessels. They're unusual, he says, in that they prevent and repair free-radical damage to the walls of those tiny vessels. Since he treats damage to vessel walls as inflammation itself — the same wall damage he calls the direct cause of atherosclerosis, coronary thrombosis and stroke — the pigments that quiet an allergy are, in his telling, guarding the blood vessels at the same time.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000814.subject: longevity
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000814.question: Can meditation lower blood pressure?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000814.answer_short: Yes—Wallach says meditation has been shown to lower blood pressure while relaxing muscles, raising DHEA, and lowering cortisol.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000814.answer_full:
Yes — Wallach says meditation has been shown to lower blood pressure, and his explanation is hormonal as much as muscular. Beyond relaxing the muscles, meditation raises circulating DHEA — what he calls the "youth hormone" — while lowering cortisol, which he describes as age-inducing. In his framing that hormonal shift supports the body's broader rejuvenating processes, which is why he presents meditation as part of an anti-aging routine rather than a standalone cure for blood pressure.

It helps to see where meditation sits in his wider view of hypertension. Wallach pins high blood pressure primarily on chronic calcium deficiency — citing McCarron's 1980 finding, which he says more than 30 later studies backed, that calcium deficiency causes it. So he treats meditation as one supportive lever alongside heavier ones like correcting calcium and mineral intake, and — since he calls obesity a serious predisposing factor — losing weight, which he says can drop elevated blood pressure dramatically.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000815.subject: longevity
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000815.question: What is a healthy blood pressure in the world's longest-lived people?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000815.answer_short: Wallach notes the long-lived Caucasus centenarians typically run a blood pressure around 104/72 at age 100.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000815.answer_full:
Wallach reports that in the long-lived Caucasus peoples — who live in simple stone houses without electricity — blood pressure typically runs about 104/72 even at age 100, far below what most of us come to accept as normal in old age.

The point he draws from this is that high blood pressure isn't an inevitable part of aging. He blames hypertension primarily on chronic calcium deficiency rather than on salt, citing McCarron's 1980 finding — backed, he says, by more than 30 later studies — that calcium deficiency causes high blood pressure, and noting that ionized calcium (the active, unbound form in the blood) runs consistently lower in people with untreated hypertension. He rejects the idea that salt is the culprit at all: he points to the Japanese, who eat about 15 grams of salt a day yet, in his telling, have 85 percent less cardiovascular disease and hypertension than Americans. In his framing these long-lived populations keep their pressure low because they stay well-mineralized — every long-lived people on earth eats red meat, poultry, fish, eggs and dairy, he says — so their bodies never run the mineral deficits he ties to high blood pressure.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000816.subject: malnutrition
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000816.question: Can a junk-food diet make you nervous and irritable?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000816.answer_short: Wallach points to McCarrison's rat experiment: rats fed a poor processed diet (white bread, margarine, sugary tea, canned meat) turned nervous, bad-tempered and even violent, while well-fed rats stayed calm -- a vivid picture of how diet shapes mood.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000816.answer_full:
Yes — and Wallach's evidence is one of nutrition's classic experiments, McCarrison's rat-feeding study. One group of rat pups was raised on a typical working-class English diet of the day: white bread, margarine, sugared tea, boiled vegetables, canned meat and cheap jams — plenty of food, but stripped of real nourishment. Those rats didn't just fall physically ill (McCarrison logged diseases of the lungs, stomach, intestines and nerves); they turned mean. They grew nervous, bit the attendants who fed them, lived unhappily crowded together, and by the sixteenth day began killing and eating the weaker animals in the cage.

The force of the picture comes from the comparison group in the same experiment. Those rats ate a Hunza-style diet — whole-grain flatbread, butter, legumes, raw carrots and cabbage, whole milk, eggs, meat and daily sunlight — and stayed calm, with no aggression and no early deaths, reaching 27 months of age (the equivalent of 55 human years) free of overt disease. For Wallach the takeaway is blunt: the only thing that differed was what went in the food bowl, so the nervousness, bad temper and even violence trace straight back to the diet of processed junk.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000817.subject: veganism
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000817.question: Can a vegan diet turn your hair gray?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000817.answer_short: Wallach says strict vegans who don't supplement heavily with minerals tend to develop gray hair (along with receding gums, anemia and more) within about five years.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000817.answer_full:
Yes — Wallach lists gray hair as one of the early signs of a strict vegan diet. His reasoning is about minerals, not vitamins: plants can't manufacture minerals, so a diet built entirely on plants leaves the body short of them — by his count, an unsupplemented vegan runs 51 to 57 of the body's essential minerals short. Because most vegans don't supplement heavily and correctly with a special emphasis on minerals, he says the shortfall shows on the body within about five years.

In his telling gray hair rarely comes alone — he groups it with a whole cluster of deficiency signs that surface in the same window: receding gums and periodontal disease, anemia, osteoporosis and arthritis, hypertension, blood sugar problems, chronic fatigue, and in the worst cases even cancer and liver cirrhosis. Wallach rejects the vegan premise outright, arguing that every long-lived population on earth eats animal foods — red meat (pork, beef, goat, lamb), poultry, fish, eggs and dairy — and pointing to vegan crusader Linda McCartney, who he says died at 56 of breast cancer.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000820.subject: phosphorus
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000820.question: Do whole grains and a high-protein diet block the minerals my gums need?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000820.answer_short: Wallach says yes — a high-protein diet plus the phytates in cereals and whole-grain flours bind calcium, iron and zinc and lower their absorption, which can loosen teeth and worsen periodontal disease.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000820.answer_full:
Yes — and Wallach pins both problems on one element: phosphorus. Phosphorus is part of most proteins, so a high-protein diet raises your phosphorus intake, and the more phosphorus you take in, the more calcium your body needs to balance it. When that demand goes unmet, he says the excess phosphorus can loosen teeth and drive periodontal disease — along with osteoporosis, arthritis and high blood pressure.

Whole grains come at the same minerals from the other side. Grains carry phosphorus as phytates — phytic acid, which Wallach identifies chemically as inositol hexaphosphate. When bread is made from unleavened whole-grain flour, that phytic acid latches onto calcium, iron, zinc and other minerals in the gut and lowers their absorption, binding calcium in particular into an insoluble salt the body can't take up. That's the twist he keeps returning to: the same phytate is a required nutrient on one hand and a mineral-robbing dietary negative on the other.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000821.subject: vitamin-c
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000821.question: Can vitamin C deficiency make my gums swell and my teeth loosen?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000821.answer_short: Yes — Wallach lists swollen and inflamed gums, bleeding gums and loose teeth among the signs of vitamin C deficiency, together with weakness, anemia and osteoporosis.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000821.answer_full:
Yes. Wallach counts swollen, inflamed gums, bleeding gums and loose teeth among the classic signs of a vitamin C shortage. The reason comes down to collagen — the structural protein that holds your gums, teeth, bones and blood-vessel walls together. Wallach explains that vitamin C is a required cofactor your body needs to build collagen, so when it runs low the connective scaffolding starts to fail: gums swell and bleed, bruises come easily, and wounds are slow to heal. He calls this the everyday, sub-scurvy face of low vitamin C — the milder version that stops short of full-blown scurvy.

The loose teeth trace to the same failing structure. Wallach notes the alveolar bone — the thin, fragile jawbone that anchors each tooth root — is so delicate that even a tiny loss of density shows up as receding gums and loose teeth long before it would in a big bone like the thigh, and osteoporosis sits right alongside gum bleeding on his deficiency list. His fix is vitamin C to bowel tolerance (raising the dose to the level your gut can comfortably handle). In his fuller list the same deficiency also brings general weakness, anemia, poor appetite and growth, and swollen wrist and ankle joints.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000824.subject: vitamin-b12
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000824.question: Why am I low in B12 even though I eat meat?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000824.answer_short: Wallach says a B12 deficiency severe enough to cause a progressive demyelinating neuropathy can develop when stomach acid is too low, intrinsic factor is missing, or celiac/Crohn's disease blocks absorption in the ileum -- not only on a vegan diet.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000824.answer_full:
Because eating meat only covers the intake side — actually absorbing that B12 is a separate job, and Wallach says it's the part that usually breaks down. Pulling B12 out of food takes an acid stomach plus a helper protein called "intrinsic factor," and the intrinsic factor is itself acid-dependent. When stomach acid runs low — the stomach's pH drifting toward neutral or alkaline — or when too little intrinsic factor is made, the B12 in your meat passes straight through unabsorbed. Wallach ties that low stomach acid most often to a salt-restricted diet, since salt is the raw material the stomach uses to manufacture its hydrochloric acid.

The absorbing machinery can also be knocked out physically. Surgery on the stomach zones that secrete intrinsic factor (the fundus and cardia), or damage to the ileum in the small intestine from celiac or Crohn's disease, blocks uptake even with plenty of B12 in the diet. Only a strict vegan — no animal products or supplements at all — is short on intake itself. Left uncorrected, the deficiency drives a megaloblastic anemia (oversized, immature red cells) and a progressive demyelinating neuropathy, meaning the myelin insulation is stripped from the nerves. Because the real bottleneck is absorption, Wallach's fixes work around the stomach: a stomach-acid substitute like betaine HCl to reactivate intrinsic factor, or B12 given by injection or under the tongue to bypass the gut entirely.

WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000826.subject: vitamin-b5
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000826.question: What causes burning feet?
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000826.answer_short: Wallach attributes burning sensations of the feet and pain in the arms and legs to a deficiency of pantothenic acid (vitamin B5), along with dermatitis and loss of appetite.
WAL-CLM-IMMORT-000826.answer_full:
Wallach traces burning feet to a deficiency of pantothenic acid — vitamin B5. In his framework B5 is indispensable because it forms part of coenzyme A, the molecule the body uses to release energy from carbohydrates, fats and proteins and to build acetylcholine, a nerve-signaling chemical. Because it's water-soluble and constantly used up, he says it has to be resupplied daily through diet and supplementation, and a shortfall announces itself out in the extremities: burning sensations in the feet and pain in the arms and legs.

In his telling burning feet rarely travels alone. Wallach lists it alongside a whole cluster of B5-deficiency signs — dermatitis (inflamed skin), loss of appetite, nausea and indigestion, muscle cramps, depression, a racing heartbeat and fainting spells — so he'd read burning feet as one flag in a larger pattern rather than an isolated complaint.
